To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the extracellular levels DA in the ventral striatum are regulated by both pre‐ and postsynaptic receptors in a complex manner that is dependent on the site of action and the concentration of the drug.
the somatodendritically released DA within the VTA is controlled via negative feedback by DA released in the ACB through D1 and D‐2 receptor‐mediated mechanisms.
the extracellular levels in the VTA of DA, which is released in the ACB in a DA uptake‐inhibitor‐dependent manner, are regulated by D1 and D‐2 receptors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of DA receptors in the nucleus acumbens in controlling negative feedback regulation of mesoaccumbal somatodendrictic DA release in the VTA of rat brain.
the control mechanisms that regulate DA release in the mesolimbic pathway and their role in the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia and depression.
the role of DA receptors in the ACB in controlling the negative feedback regulation of mesoacumbens DA release in the VTA of the rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DA release in the VTA is controlled by a negative feedback pathway involving D1 and D 2 receptors in the ACB.
the D1 and D 2 receptors in the ACB are involved in the regulation of the extracellular levels and turnover of DA in the mesolimbic DA system.

DA release in the ACB is subject to a negative feedback control by DA release in the VTA, which is mediated by D1 receptors in the VTA and by both D1 and, to a greater degree, D2 receptors in the ACB.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the somatodendritically released DA in the VSA is regulated by a long‐loop feedback pathway originating from the ACB.
the mesoaccumbens pathway is an important part of a negative feedback loop that modulates somatodendrtic DA release in the VTA.

DA release in the ACB is controlled by a combination of presynaptic and postsynaptic DA receptor mechanisms, whereas DA release in the VTA is controlled by both presynaptic and long‐loop postsynaptic mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that

DA receptors in the ACB are involved in controlling negative feedback regulation of DA release in the VTA, and the results provide a basis for understanding the role of DA receptors in the pathophysiology of drug dependence.
DA release in the ACB is controlled in part by a negative feedback loop involving DA receptors in the VTA.
DA release in the ACB is under the negative feedback regulation of mesoacumbal DA neurons.
